# Diastasis Recti Screening Protocol
### For Use Alongside the 4-Week On-Ramp Block

## Your Scope First — This Matters

Before anything else, be clear with yourself and with her about what you are and are not doing here. As a personal trainer you are **not diagnosing diastasis recti**. What you are doing is conducting an informal functional screen that tells you whether the exercises you are programming are appropriate, whether you need to modify them, and critically, whether you need to refer her to a women's health physiotherapist for formal assessment. That referral pathway is not a last resort — it is a normal and expected part of postpartum care, and framing it that way to her removes any stigma or alarm from the conversation.

A women's health physiotherapist can assess inter-recti distance with real-time ultrasound, evaluate linea alba tension and load transfer capacity, assess the pelvic floor simultaneously, and give a clinical picture that no amount of trainer screening can replicate. If she has not seen one yet, the recommendation to do so should happen regardless of what your screen finds. It is simply good postpartum practice.

---

## Understanding What You Are Actually Screening For

This is worth getting right conceptually because the field has moved significantly in the last decade and some of the information still circulating among trainers is outdated.

The old model treated diastasis recti as a gap measurement problem. If the gap between the two rectus columns was wider than two finger-widths, it was classified as diastasis and treated as pathological. This led to enormous anxiety among postpartum women who were told they had a condition that needed fixing, and to overly restrictive exercise prescriptions that were not always warranted.

The current clinical understanding is more nuanced. **Gap width alone is a poor predictor of function.** What matters more is the **tension and load transfer capacity of the linea alba** — whether the connective tissue between the two rectus columns can stiffen appropriately under load to transfer force between the left and right sides of the trunk. A woman can have a measurable gap and excellent linea alba tension with no functional impairment whatsoever. Conversely, a woman can have a narrow gap with poor tension and significant difficulty managing intra-abdominal pressure.

What this means practically is that your screen is looking for **two things simultaneously**: the presence and approximate width of any separation, and the functional behaviour of the midline under load. The second of these is more important for your programming decisions than the first.

---

## When to Screen

**Initial screen:** Conduct this at the start of Week 1, before the first acclimatisation session. This gives you a baseline and informs how cautiously you approach even the gentle Week 1 work.

**Progress screen:** Repeat at the start of Week 3, when she hits 12 weeks postpartum and you are considering progressing the core work and introducing cardio.

**End-of-block screen:** Repeat at the end of Week 4 as part of the overall block assessment before designing the next phase.

Do not screen mid-session when she is fatigued. Always screen at the beginning of a session before any exercise has been performed.

---

## The Screening Process — Step by Step

### Part One — The Conversation

Before you touch anything, ask her the following questions and note the answers. These are not just formalities — they give you clinical context that changes how you interpret the physical findings.

Does she notice any doming, coning, or ridge appearing down the centre of her abdomen during any movement — getting up from lying, lifting, coughing, or sneezing? Does she have any sensation of weakness or instability through the middle of her trunk? Does she experience any lower back pain that feels different from general postpartum muscle soreness? Does she have any pelvic floor symptoms — leaking, heaviness, or pressure — during daily activities, not just exercise? Has she had any previous abdominal surgery, including her caesarean if applicable?

The presence of doming during daily activities like getting up from bed is a significant finding. It suggests the linea alba is under load in functional contexts, not just during exercise, and warrants a more conservative approach and an earlier referral.

---

### Part Two — The Resting Palpation Check

Have her lie supine with knees bent and feet flat, in the same position as the breath reset. Ask her to breathe normally and relax completely. You are going to palpate the linea alba — the vertical midline of the abdomen — to identify the resting state of the tissue before any load is applied.

Place two fingers horizontally across the midline, just above the navel. Apply gentle downward pressure. You are feeling for the edges of the rectus abdominis on either side. In a woman without any separation, the tissue will feel relatively firm and the two columns will be close together or touching. If there is a separation, your fingers will sink into a softer channel between the two columns.

**Note the following:**

*Width:* How many finger-widths fit comfortably in the gap? One finger-width is approximately 1 cm. A gap of up to 2 cm (roughly two finger-widths) at rest is within the range of normal variation at this postpartum stage. A gap of 2–3 cm warrants monitoring and conservative programming. A gap greater than 3 cm warrants referral to a women's health physiotherapist before progressing the core programme, though it does not mean stopping exercise entirely.

*Depth:* How far do your fingers sink before they meet resistance? Shallow sinking with firm resistance at the base suggests reasonable linea alba tension even if a gap is present. Fingers sinking deeply with little resistance suggests poor tension and is the more concerning finding functionally.

*Symmetry:* Is the gap consistent along the length of the midline, or is it wider in some areas than others? Check at three points — 2 cm above the navel, at the navel, and 2 cm below the navel. The gap is typically widest at or just above the navel. A gap that is significantly wider below the navel than above it is worth noting specifically for the physiotherapist.

Repeat this palpation on both sides of the midline and note whether the tissue feels symmetric.

---

### Part Three — The Active Loading Test

This is where you assess linea alba tension under load, which as noted above is more functionally relevant than the resting gap measurement alone.

Ask her to perform a **partial curl-up** — not a full crunch, just a very slow lift of the head and shoulders off the floor until the shoulder blades begin to clear the surface. She should exhale slowly as she does this. You are watching and feeling simultaneously.

**What you are watching for:**

*Doming or coning:* A visible ridge or tent shape appearing along the midline as she lifts. This indicates that intra-abdominal pressure is being directed outward through the linea alba rather than being managed by the surrounding musculature. This is the key visual sign of poor load transfer capacity.

*Asymmetry:* One side of the abdomen appearing to work harder than the other, or the midline deviating to one side.

*Breath holding:* If she holds her breath to initiate the movement, the intra-abdominal pressure demand is already exceeding her management capacity at this very low load. This is important information.

**What you are feeling for:**

Keep your fingers lightly on the midline during the movement. As she lifts, the linea alba should stiffen — you should feel the tissue become firmer under your fingers and the edges of the gap, if present, should become more defined rather than softer. This stiffening response is the functional indicator you are looking for. If the tissue remains soft or your fingers sink further as she lifts, tension generation is poor regardless of the resting gap width.

**After the active test**, ask her to return to lying and perform the same partial curl-up again, this time with a deliberate exhale and gentle pelvic floor engagement before she initiates the movement. Note whether the midline behaviour changes with the breath and pelvic floor cue. In many cases it will improve noticeably, which tells you that the neuromuscular connection is present but needs reinforcement — a very positive finding.

---

### Part Four — The Functional Movement Screen

The partial curl-up is a direct test but it is not a functional one — nobody needs to do a curl-up in daily life. These two additional checks give you information about how the midline behaves under the kinds of loads she will actually encounter in the programme.

**Quadruped hold:** Ask her to come onto all fours in the bird dog starting position and hold for 5 breath cycles. Watch the midline from the side. Any visible sag or dome through the abdomen suggests the anti-extension demand of quadruped is already challenging her load management. If this is present, the bird dog progressions in the core programme need to start at Level 1 and progress very slowly.

**Heel slide with observation:** Ask her to perform 5 heel slides each side as in the Week 1 programme. Watch the midline and the lower back. Any doming, any lower back lift, or any visible asymmetry in how the two sides of the abdomen respond tells you the heel slide is already a meaningful load for her system. This is not a reason to avoid it — it is a reason to cue the breath and pelvic floor engagement more explicitly and to watch carefully as you progress.

---

## Recording Your Findings

Keep a simple written record after each screen. You do not need clinical terminology — you need enough information to track change over time and to communicate clearly with a physiotherapist if you refer. A useful format is as follows.

**Date and postpartum age.** Resting gap: location, approximate width in finger-widths, depth and quality of tissue resistance. Active loading test: doming present or absent, tissue stiffening response present or absent, breath holding present or absent. Response to breath and pelvic floor cue: improved, unchanged, or worsened. Functional screen findings: quadruped and heel slide observations. Subjective report: any symptoms she mentions. Overall impression and programming implications.

---

## Interpreting Your Findings and What to Do With Them

### Finding: No visible gap, tissue stiffens well under load, no doming, no symptoms

This is the most straightforward picture. Proceed with the programme as written. Continue monitoring at the scheduled screen points. Encourage her to see a women's health physiotherapist anyway as a positive check-in rather than a problem-solving visit.

---

### Finding: Gap present (up to 2–3 finger-widths), tissue stiffens reasonably under load, no doming, no symptoms

This is a common finding at 10 weeks postpartum and does not require significant programme modification. The gap itself is less important than the functional behaviour. Proceed with the programme but be more attentive to midline behaviour during the core progressions. Avoid any exercise that produces doming. Refer to a women's health physiotherapist for formal assessment and reassurance — frame this as routine rather than alarming.

**Specific programming notes:** Dead bug progressions are appropriate but watch carefully at each level before advancing. Plank from toes is fine if breathing is continuous and no doming is visible. Carries are appropriate and beneficial. Avoid any loaded spinal flexion — this is already excluded from the programme but worth reinforcing.

---

### Finding: Gap present, poor tissue stiffening under load, doming visible during active test, symptoms present during daily activities

This warrants a more conservative approach and a prompt referral. Do not stop exercise — complete rest is not indicated and is likely counterproductive — but modify the programme as follows.

Keep all core work at the lower progression levels until a physiotherapist has assessed her and given guidance. Specifically, stay at dead bug Level 1 and 2, bird dog Level 1 and 2, and plank from knees only. Avoid the pallof press until tension improves. The carries are likely fine as they are anti-lateral flexion rather than anti-extension, but monitor carefully. Prioritise the breath and pelvic floor coordination work above everything else — this is the foundation that needs to be more solid before load is added.

Refer to a women's health physiotherapist as a priority rather than a routine recommendation. Be clear with her that this is not alarming — it is simply the appropriate clinical support for what you are finding, and the physiotherapist can give her a much more complete picture than you can.

---

### Finding: Gap greater than 3 finger-widths, fingers sink deeply with little resistance, doming present, symptoms during daily activities

Refer before progressing the core programme. Continue with the gentle movement work from Week 1 — the breath reset, glute bridges, heel slides, and walking — as these are low enough load to be appropriate in almost all cases. But do not advance the core progressions until she has been seen by a physiotherapist and you have their guidance. This is not a crisis — it is a clinical situation that is outside your scope to manage independently, and the right thing to do is say so clearly and supportively.

---

## What to Tell Her

How you frame this conversation matters enormously. Postpartum women are already navigating enormous physical and psychological change, and the word diastasis carries a lot of anxiety in online communities — much of it based on the outdated gap-measurement model described earlier.

Tell her that you are going to check in on how her midline is responding to exercise at regular points throughout the programme, because this is normal good practice for postpartum training and gives you information that helps you programme appropriately for her. Tell her that having some separation is extremely common — the majority of women have some degree of inter-recti distance at this stage — and that what matters far more than whether a gap exists is how the tissue functions under load. Tell her that if you find anything that suggests she would benefit from seeing a women's health physiotherapist, that is a positive step toward getting the right support, not a sign that something is seriously wrong.

The goal is that she feels monitored and supported, not surveilled and anxious. The screen is a tool for better programming, not a source of new worry.

---

## Referral Triggers — Summary

Refer to a women's health physiotherapist if any of the following are present at any screen point:

Resting gap greater than 3 finger-widths at any location along the midline. Poor or absent tissue stiffening response under load regardless of gap width. Visible doming during the active loading test that does not resolve with breath and pelvic floor cueing. Any pelvic floor symptoms — leaking, heaviness, pressure, or pain — during the screening exercises or reported during daily activities. Lower back or pelvic girdle pain that is not resolving or is worsening. Any finding that you are uncertain how to interpret or programme around. And as noted above — even in the absence of any of these findings, a routine check-in with a women's health physiotherapist at some point during this block is simply good postpartum care and worth recommending to every client in this situation.

# Managing Intensity Progression at Mid-Week 2
### 11 Weeks Postpartum — Feeling Good Is Data, Not a Green Light

## The Honest Answer First

Yes, with important caveats — and the caveats matter enough that they need to come before the programming changes.

Feeling great at 11 weeks postpartum is genuinely good news and reflects well on how the first week and a half has gone. But it is also one of the most common precursors to setbacks in postpartum recovery, and not because the woman did anything wrong. The mechanism is straightforward: the systems that generate subjective wellbeing — mood, energy, motivation, confidence — recover faster than the systems that govern connective tissue remodelling, pelvic floor neuromuscular function, and hormonal stabilisation. She feels ready before she is fully ready, and the gap between those two things is where overload injuries and pelvic floor symptom flare-ups tend to occur.

This is not a reason to ignore how she feels. Subjective wellbeing is real data and it matters. It just needs to be interpreted alongside the objective data from your screens and session observations rather than in isolation.

The question to ask is not **can we push intensity** but rather **which specific parameters can we increase, by how much, and what are we watching for when we do.**

---

## What "Intensity" Actually Means Here

Before changing anything, be precise about which variable you are talking about. Intensity is not a single dial — it is several independent parameters that can be adjusted separately and that carry different risk profiles at this stage.

**Load** — the weight on the dumbbell. Increasing this raises the mechanical demand on the musculoskeletal system and the intra-abdominal pressure management demand on the pelvic floor. Moderate risk if progressed carefully.

**Volume** — total sets and reps. Increasing this raises cumulative fatigue and tissue load. Lower risk than load in the short term but can accumulate across a week and affect recovery.

**Tempo** — the speed of movement. Slowing the eccentric phase increases time under tension without adding load. Low risk and high value at this stage — this is the best intensity lever to pull first.

**Density** — how much work is done in a given time, usually by reducing rest periods. Moderate risk because it raises cardiovascular demand and reduces recovery between sets, which can affect technique and pelvic floor management.

**Exercise complexity** — moving to a harder variation. Risk depends entirely on the specific exercise and what the screen findings show.

**Session frequency** — adding a fourth session. Not appropriate this week. Three sessions remains the right frequency at 11 weeks postpartum regardless of how good she feels.

The safest and most productive approach right now is to pull the **tempo and load levers first**, leave volume largely unchanged, and not touch density or frequency.

---

## What the Mid-Week 2 Picture Should Tell You

Before making any changes, run a quick informal check across three areas.

**Session observations:** Has there been any doming, any breath holding, any reported symptoms during or after sessions? If the answer to all three is no, that is a genuine green light for modest progression. If there has been any of these, even mild and transient, the programme is already at the right level and the feeling-great report is the nervous system recovering ahead of the connective tissue — hold the line.

**Pelvic floor report:** Ask her directly. Any leaking, heaviness, or dragging in the 24 hours after either session so far? Any change in pelvic floor symptoms compared to before the programme started? A no here supports progression. Any yes warrants staying exactly where you are.

**Energy and sleep:** Is she feeling great because sleep has been better this week, or because the training is genuinely feeling easy? Both are valid but they suggest different responses. Better sleep is wonderful but it is not a training adaptation — it is a variable that will fluctuate. If the sessions feel easy because the movement patterns are becoming automatic and the loads feel light, that is a training adaptation and it does support modest progression.

---

## The Specific Changes to Make

### Load — Yes, With Conditions

For the lower body exercises — the Romanian deadlift and the reverse lunge — if she has been using 2–4 kg dumbbells and technique is clean with no symptoms, moving to 4–6 kg is appropriate. This is the progression that was already planned for Week 3, brought forward by approximately one week. It is not an aggressive jump.

For upper body — the bent-over row and shoulder press — hold at the current load for now. The upper body exercises are already at an appropriate stimulus level and the pelvic floor demand of upper body pressing and pulling, while lower than lower body work, is still present. There is no compelling reason to increase upper body load mid-week 2.

For the glute bridge — if she has been doing the bilateral bridge with a 3-second hold and it feels genuinely easy, you can introduce the **single-leg glute bridge** now rather than waiting for Week 3. This is a complexity increase rather than a load increase and carries a low risk profile. Apply the same technique standards — level hips, continuous breathing, no lower back compensation.

**The condition on all load increases:** The first set at the new weight is an assessment set. Watch everything — midline, breathing, technique, her face. If anything changes negatively, the new weight stays for that exercise and you reassess next session.

---

### Tempo — The Best Lever Right Now

This is the change that will give her the most meaningful increase in training stimulus with the lowest risk profile, and it is worth explaining why so she does not feel like she is being managed down.

Slowing the eccentric phase of any exercise — the lowering phase of a squat, the descent of a Romanian deadlift, the lowering phase of a push-up — increases time under tension, recruits more motor units, causes greater mechanical disruption to the muscle tissue that drives adaptation, and actually reduces peak intra-abdominal pressure compared to faster, more ballistic movement. It is harder and safer simultaneously, which is a rare combination.

**Apply the following tempo changes from the next session:**

Goblet squat and chair squat: 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at the bottom, drive up. Previously she was likely squatting at a natural tempo of 1–2 seconds down.

Romanian deadlift: 3 seconds to hinge down, 1 second pause at the bottom of the range, drive up through the hips.

Reverse lunge: 3 seconds to lower, 1 second pause at the bottom, drive up.

Push-up or wall push-up: 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at the chest, exhale to push.

Bent-over row: 2 seconds to lower the dumbbell, 1 second pause, exhale to row.

These tempo changes alone will make the existing sessions feel significantly more demanding without changing a single other variable. If she reports that the sessions feel much harder after the tempo change, that is the appropriate response and no further intensity increase is needed this week.

---

### Core — One Progression Available

If the mid-week 2 core work has been symptom-free and the linea alba is behaving well under load, you can advance one level in the dead bug progression — moving from the leg-only variation to the contralateral arm and leg version if she has not already reached it. Do not advance the plank or side plank this week — those progressions are appropriately timed for Week 3.

The pallof press can move from the hold to the press if the hold has felt easy across both sessions. Two seconds out, two seconds hold, two seconds return. This is a meaningful increase in anti-rotation demand and is appropriate if the hold has been genuinely comfortable.

---

### What Not to Change

Do not reduce rest periods. At 11 weeks postpartum, rest periods serve a recovery function that goes beyond simple cardiovascular recovery — they allow the pelvic floor to return to a resting state between sets, which matters for cumulative load management across a session. Sixty seconds between lower body sets stays at sixty seconds.

Do not add sets. The volume is appropriate for this stage. Adding sets to chase a training effect is the kind of decision that feels fine in the session and shows up as fatigue or symptoms two days later.

Do not add a fourth session. Three sessions per week is the right frequency. If she has energy to spare, direct it toward the longer walks and the stationary bike work that is coming in Week 3 — that is a better use of the additional capacity than a fourth strength session.

Do not introduce any new exercises that were planned for Week 3 or 4 beyond the single-leg glute bridge noted above. The programme is sequenced deliberately and the sequencing reflects tissue readiness, not just fitness readiness.

---

## How to Frame This With Her

She is feeling great and she wants to work harder. That is a fantastic sign and you should tell her so genuinely. The conversation to have is something like this.

The fact that you are feeling this good at 11 weeks is really positive and it tells us the first week and a half has been exactly right for you. What I want to do is make the sessions feel more challenging in a way that keeps building the foundation rather than jumping ahead of it. We are going to slow the tempo on your main lifts, which sounds simple but will make a real difference to how the sessions feel. We are also going to nudge the load up on your lower body work. What we are not going to do is add more sessions or cut your rest periods, because those changes carry a different kind of risk at this stage and the gains are not worth it yet. In two weeks, if everything continues to look and feel this good, the programme opens up considerably.

That framing does three things. It validates her experience, it gives her a concrete and honest explanation of the decision, and it gives her a near-term horizon — two weeks — that makes the current boundaries feel temporary rather than indefinite.

---

## The Underlying Principle

The postpartum body does not adapt on the same timeline as a rested, non-postpartum body. The connective tissue remodelling that determines whether the linea alba, the pelvic floor fascia, and the joint ligaments can handle progressive load is governed by hormonal and biological processes that do not accelerate in response to motivation or positive affect. The training stimulus can be increased modestly when the objective markers support it. The biological timeline cannot be shortened regardless of how good she feels.

Feeling great is the goal. It is also, at this specific stage, a reason to be thoughtful rather than a reason to push. The women who are still training well at six months, twelve months, and five years postpartum are almost always the ones who were patient in the first three months. That is the outcome worth optimising for.

# HIIT, Fat Loss, and Postpartum Reality
### The Conversation You Need to Have Before You Programme Anything

## This One Needs Pushing Back On — Respectfully but Clearly

This is the moment where being a good trainer means saying something she might not want to hear, and saying it in a way that keeps her engaged and motivated rather than dismissed. Because the honest answer is not *here is your HIIT programme* — it is *here is why HIIT for fat loss is the wrong goal framed in the wrong way at the wrong time, and here is what will actually get you where you want to go.*

That is not a reason to refuse to help her. It is a reason to reframe the conversation before touching the programme.

---

## The Fat Loss Conversation First

### Why This Goal Needs Reframing Right Now

She is 11 weeks postpartum. Her body is doing something extraordinary and metabolically expensive — recovering from pregnancy and birth, potentially producing milk, remodelling connective tissue, regulating hormones that are still nowhere near their pre-pregnancy baseline, and doing all of this on fragmented sleep. Pursuing fat loss as a primary goal in this context is not just premature — it can actively work against the recovery processes that will determine her long-term health and body composition.

The specific mechanisms are worth understanding.

**Cortisol and the postpartum hormonal environment.** HIIT is a significant cortisol stressor. In a well-rested, hormonally stable person, the cortisol spike from a HIIT session is acute, resolves within hours, and contributes to positive adaptations. In a postpartum woman at 11 weeks, cortisol is already chronically elevated from sleep deprivation, physical recovery demands, and the psychological load of new parenthood. Adding repeated high-intensity cortisol spikes on top of a chronically elevated baseline does not produce the same adaptive response — it produces accumulated stress load that impairs recovery, disrupts sleep further, and can suppress the immune system. The fat loss effect she associates with HIIT from her pre-pregnancy experience will not replicate in this hormonal context.

**Breastfeeding, if applicable.** If she is breastfeeding, aggressive caloric restriction combined with high-intensity exercise is associated with reduced milk supply and altered milk composition. Her body will prioritise milk production over fat mobilisation, and the combination of restriction and high intensity can trigger a stress response that makes both goals harder to achieve simultaneously.

**Relative energy deficiency.** Postpartum women are at meaningful risk of relative energy deficiency — a state where energy availability is insufficient to support both the demands of exercise and the demands of normal physiological function including recovery and hormonal regulation. The symptoms overlap significantly with normal new-parent experience — fatigue, mood changes, disrupted sleep — which makes it easy to miss. Pursuing fat loss through caloric restriction plus high-intensity exercise is the most direct route to this state.

**The body composition picture will change anyway.** This is perhaps the most important thing to tell her. The hormonal shifts of the postpartum period — particularly the decline of relaxin and the gradual return of oestrogen toward pre-pregnancy levels — drive significant spontaneous body composition changes between roughly 3 and 12 months postpartum in women who are eating adequately and exercising appropriately. The progressive strength training she is already doing is building lean tissue that will increase her resting metabolic rate. The walking and low-intensity cardio is supporting fat oxidation without the cortisol cost of HIIT. She is already doing the things that will produce the outcome she wants — she just cannot see it yet because 11 weeks is too early.

---

### What to Actually Say to Her

Do not lecture. Do not make her feel judged for wanting to look and feel like herself again — that is a completely understandable and legitimate desire. The framing that tends to land is something like this.

*I hear you, and I want to help you get there. The honest thing I can tell you is that HIIT for fat loss right now is likely to slow down the result you want rather than speed it up, and here is why. Your body is still in recovery mode — the hormones, the connective tissue, the pelvic floor — and high-intensity work at this stage tends to add to the stress load rather than produce the adaptation you remember from before. What you are already doing is genuinely building the foundation for the body composition changes you want. In four to six weeks, when we are past the 16-week mark and your pelvic floor benchmarks are solid, we can start introducing higher intensity work in a way that will actually produce the result. Right now, pushing too hard too soon is the one thing most likely to set that timeline back.*

Then give her something. Do not just say no — give her a concrete plan for when and how HIIT comes back, and give her something that scratches the itch in the meantime.

---

## What Is Actually Safe Right Now — The Honest Intensity Ceiling

At 11–14 weeks postpartum, the evidence-informed ceiling for cardiovascular intensity is **moderate — roughly 6 to 7 out of 10 perceived exertion** for the majority of the session, with brief excursions to 7–8 on specific efforts. This is not HIIT. It is not nothing either.

The no-jumping restriction from the OB runs through Week 4 of this block — until approximately 14 weeks postpartum. This rules out any impact-based HIIT format: no jumping jacks, no jump squats, no burpees, no skipping, no running intervals. These are not excluded because of fitness — they are excluded because the pelvic floor load of repeated ground impact before the tissue is ready is a genuine injury risk.

After 14 weeks, and only after passing the pelvic floor benchmarks described in the screening protocol, low-impact higher intensity work can be introduced gradually. True HIIT — the format she remembers from spin class and pre-pregnancy training — is realistically a 16 to 20 week postpartum conversation, not an 11 week one.

---

## What to Add Right Now — Scratching the Itch Appropriately

Here is what can be slotted into the existing programme to give her more cardiovascular stimulus and a sense of working hard, without the pelvic floor risk or the cortisol cost of true HIIT.

### Option 1 — Tempo Circuits Within Strength Sessions

This is the most immediately available option and requires no changes to the programme structure. Rather than performing the strength exercises as straight sets with rest, two or three exercises can be paired as a circuit with a short rest between rounds. The cardiovascular demand increases meaningfully, the session feels more like the training she remembers, and the load on the pelvic floor remains manageable because the exercises are already screened and appropriate.

**Example circuit for Week 3 Session A:**

Perform the following three exercises back to back with no rest between exercises. Rest 75 seconds between rounds. Complete 3 rounds.

Goblet squat, 10 reps. Immediately into dumbbell bent-over row, 10 reps each side. Immediately into forearm plank hold, 5 breath cycles.

Rest 75 seconds. Repeat.

This will elevate her heart rate into the 130–150 bpm range for most people at this fitness level, which is a genuine cardiovascular stimulus. It does not involve impact, does not involve maximal effort, and does not require any new exercises. It simply reorganises what is already there.

Apply this to one session per week in Week 3, and two sessions per week in Week 4 if Week 3 goes well and there are no symptoms.

---

### Option 2 — Stationary Bike Intervals (Week 3 Onwards)

As already outlined in the cardio section, the stationary bike is the most appropriate bridge toward her spinning background. In Week 3 the prescription was steady state at 5–6 out of 10. That can be modified slightly to include very mild intensity variation that gives her a taste of interval work without the physiological cost of true HIIT.

**Week 3 bike session — modified:**

5 minutes easy warm-up, perceived exertion 4/10.
Then 5 rounds of: 3 minutes at 6/10, 2 minutes at 4/10.
5 minutes easy cool-down.
Total: 35 minutes.

This is not HIIT. The work intervals are moderate, not maximal, and the recovery intervals are genuine recovery. But it has the structural feel of interval training and will produce a cardiovascular response that is meaningfully different from pure steady state. For a former spinner, the psychological effect of doing something that resembles interval work should not be underestimated.

**Week 4 bike session — progressed:**

5 minutes easy warm-up.
Then 4 rounds of: 4 minutes at 7/10, 2 minutes at 4/10.
5 minutes easy cool-down.
Total: 37 minutes.

The 7/10 efforts are approaching the lower boundary of high intensity. She will feel these. They are still seated, still controlled, and still within the appropriate ceiling for this stage. This is as close to HIIT as the programme gets before 14 weeks postpartum.

---

### Option 3 — Low-Impact Cardio Intervals on Non-Strength Days

From Week 3 onwards, one non-strength day per week can include a low-impact interval session. This uses the walk-based interval structure from the cardio section but progresses it toward something that feels more like a workout.

**Week 3 — power walk intervals:**

5 minutes easy. Then 6 rounds of 2 minutes at the fastest walking pace she can sustain — arms pumping, purposeful stride, breathing hard but not gasping — followed by 90 seconds easy. 5 minutes easy cool-down. Total approximately 30 minutes.

At a genuine power walking pace, heart rate will reach 130–145 bpm for most people. This is aerobic interval training. It is not HIIT and should not be sold as such, but it is a real cardiovascular stimulus and it is appropriate right now.

**Week 4 — progress to include gentle inclines if available:**

Same structure but incorporate any available gentle hills or use a treadmill incline of 4–6% during the work intervals. The incline increases cardiovascular demand without adding impact. Monitor pelvic floor symptoms carefully — incline walking increases intra-abdominal pressure more than flat walking and this is the first time she will encounter that stimulus in a structured way.

---

## The HIIT Return Plan — Give Her the Horizon

She needs to know this is not a permanent no. Here is a concrete timeline to give her.

**14 weeks postpartum — end of this block:**
If pelvic floor benchmarks are passed, the OB restriction on jumping lifts. Low-impact higher intensity work is appropriate. The bike intervals can progress to include short higher effort efforts of 8/10. Power walking intervals can extend. No impact yet.

**16 weeks postpartum:**
If symptom-free throughout the preceding two weeks and the pelvic floor screen remains clean, introduce a **return-to-impact protocol.** This is a graduated process — not jumping straight into a HIIT class — that begins with jogging on the spot, progresses to short jog intervals, and builds over two to three weeks before any class environment is considered. The Groom, Donnelly and Brockwell return-to-running guidelines apply here and are worth following explicitly.

**18–20 weeks postpartum:**
If the return-to-impact protocol has gone well and she is running or jogging without symptoms, a modified HIIT session can be introduced — one session per week, lower volume than pre-pregnancy, with impact elements included but not dominant. This might look like a 20-minute session with bodyweight squats, step-based movements, light dumbbell work, and short jog intervals rather than a full pre-pregnancy HIIT class.

**20–24 weeks postpartum:**
Return to spin class is realistic if all the preceding stages have been symptom-free. First two or three classes treated as assessment sessions — seated throughout, own pace, monitoring symptoms.

**The full pre-pregnancy HIIT programme:**
Realistically 6 months postpartum at the earliest for most women, and only if the pelvic floor has been consistently symptom-free. This is not a pessimistic timeline — it is an honest one, and women who follow it tend to return to full training permanently rather than cycling through flare-ups and setbacks.

---

## Revised Weekly Structure With Cardio Intensity Additions

Here is how the full week looks with these additions slotted in, for Weeks 3 and 4 specifically since that is where the new elements appear.

**Week 3 — Sample Week**

Monday: Strength Session A with tempo circuit format for two exercise pairings.
Tuesday: Power walk intervals, 30 minutes.
Wednesday: Rest or gentle walk.
Thursday: Strength Session B, straight sets.
Friday: Stationary bike, 35 minutes with mild intervals as described above.
Saturday: Strength Session C, straight sets.
Sunday: Rest.

Total training sessions: six, but two of those are low-intensity cardio and one is moderate. The actual stress load is appropriate.

**Week 4 — Sample Week**

Monday: Strength Session A with tempo circuit format.
Tuesday: Power walk intervals with incline, 30–35 minutes.
Wednesday: Rest or gentle walk.
Thursday: Strength Session B with tempo circuit format.
Friday: Stationary bike, 37 minutes with Week 4 interval structure.
Saturday: Strength Session C, straight sets.
Sunday: Rest.

---

## The Number She Actually Needs to Hear

If the fat loss conversation needs a concrete anchor, give her this one. Research on postpartum body composition consistently shows that the single strongest predictor of favourable body composition at 12 months postpartum is **not exercise intensity** — it is **sleep quality, stress load, and dietary adequacy.** A woman who sleeps reasonably well, eats enough protein, manages her stress load, and does moderate progressive exercise will have better body composition outcomes at one year than a woman who does aggressive HIIT on poor sleep with a caloric deficit. The biology is unambiguous on this.

She cannot fully control her sleep right now. She can control whether she adds a high cortisol training stress on top of an already stressed system. Framing the current programme not as a limitation but as the most evidence-based route to the outcome she wants — because it genuinely is — is the most honest and motivating thing you can tell her.

# Return to Running — Postpartum Pathway
### With a 10k Autumn Goal

## The First Question — When Is Autumn?

This matters more than it might seem. The difference between a September 10k and a November 10k could be the difference between a realistic, well-prepared race and a rushed return that sets her back. Before mapping anything out, get a specific date. Then count backwards from race day to today and establish how many weeks you are actually working with.

For the purposes of this plan, the following assumes a **late October or early November race**, which from 11 weeks postpartum gives approximately **28 to 32 weeks of total preparation time**. That is a workable timeline — not generous, but workable if the return to running is managed well in the early stages. A September race would require a more direct conversation about whether the goal is the right goal for this year, or whether a spring race might serve her better. That conversation is addressed at the end of this document.

---

## What the Evidence Says About Returning to Running Postpartum

The landmark reference here is the **Groom, Donnelly and Brockwell 2019 guidelines**, which remain the most widely cited clinical framework for postpartum return to running. Their headline position is that running should not be introduced before **12 weeks postpartum at the absolute earliest**, and only then if a series of functional benchmarks are met. The 12-week figure is a floor, not a target — many women are not ready at 12 weeks and that is entirely normal.

The reasoning is biomechanical and hormonal simultaneously. Running involves a single-leg stance phase in which the pelvic floor must manage ground reaction forces of approximately **2.5 times bodyweight** with every stride. At 11 weeks postpartum, the pelvic floor musculature, the connective tissue of the pelvic girdle, and the linea alba are all still in active remodelling phases. Relaxin — the hormone that increases connective tissue laxity during pregnancy — remains elevated in breastfeeding women for the duration of lactation, which means joint and fascial stability is genuinely reduced compared to pre-pregnancy baseline regardless of how strong she feels.

The guidelines also make a point that is worth sharing with her directly: **there is no evidence that returning to running earlier produces better long-term running outcomes.** The women who return gradually and systematically are the ones who run consistently at 12 months, 2 years, and beyond. The women who rush the return are disproportionately represented in the population presenting to physiotherapists with pelvic organ prolapse, stress urinary incontinence, and pelvic girdle pain at 6 and 12 months postpartum.

---

## The Functional Benchmarks — She Must Pass These Before Running Starts

These are drawn directly from the Groom, Donnelly and Brockwell guidelines and represent the minimum functional standard for safe return to running. They are not fitness tests — a very fit woman can fail them, and passing them is about tissue readiness, not cardiovascular capacity.

All of the following should be performed **without any leaking, heaviness, dragging, pelvic or lower back pain, or pelvic floor symptoms during or for up to 30 minutes after:**

**Walking:** 30 minutes at a brisk pace on varied terrain without symptoms. She is likely already passing this given her current programme.

**Single-leg balance:** 10 seconds each side with eyes open, on a firm surface. Watch for pelvic drop on the standing side — this indicates hip abductor weakness that will become a running injury risk.

**Single-leg calf raise:** 10 repetitions each side through full range. This tests the capacity of the posterior chain to manage the propulsive demands of running.

**Single-leg bridge:** 10 repetitions each side with level hips and no compensatory trunk movement. Already in the programme from Week 3.

**Jog on the spot:** 1 minute at a light pace. This is the first impact test and should not be attempted before 12 weeks postpartum. Watch for any pelvic floor symptoms and ask her to report any heaviness or leaking during or after.

**Forward bounds:** 10 repetitions each side — a single-leg hop forward, landing and absorbing on the same leg. This tests single-leg impact absorption capacity and is a higher demand than jogging on the spot.

**Running on the spot:** 1 minute at a faster cadence than the jog. Higher impact demand than jogging on the spot.

**Hop in place:** 10 repetitions each side. Single-leg impact in a more vertical plane.

The first four benchmarks should be assessed at the **end of Week 4** of the current block — approximately 14 weeks postpartum. The impact-based benchmarks — jog on the spot onwards — should be assessed at **16 weeks postpartum** at the earliest, which falls in the first two weeks of whatever programme block follows this one.

If she cannot pass any benchmark, that benchmark becomes a training target before running begins. A failed single-leg calf raise means calf raise progressions are added to the programme. A failed single-leg balance with pelvic drop means hip abductor work is prioritised. The benchmarks are diagnostic as much as they are gatekeeping.

---

## The Women's Health Physiotherapist Appointment

This is non-negotiable in the context of a running goal. She needs a formal pelvic floor assessment from a women's health physiotherapist **before she begins the return-to-running protocol**, ideally at around **14 to 16 weeks postpartum**. This appointment should include internal pelvic floor assessment if she consents, evaluation of any diastasis, assessment of pelvic girdle stability, and specific clearance for running.

Frame this to her not as a hurdle but as the appointment that gives her the most accurate possible picture of her readiness and the most personalised guidance for her return. A physiotherapist who knows her pelvic floor status can tell her things about her running readiness that no amount of external observation can reveal. Given the 10k goal, this appointment is an investment in the race, not a bureaucratic step.

If she has not already booked this appointment, the time to book it is now, targeting a date around 14 to 16 weeks postpartum — which is two to four weeks from now.

## The Full Timeline — Week by Week

### Current Position — Weeks 1 to 4 of On-Ramp Block (10–14 Weeks Postpartum)

No running. No impact. This is already established. The work being done right now — the single-leg glute bridges, the Romanian deadlifts, the reverse lunges, the step-ups, the carries, the pelvic floor coordination — is directly building the foundation that running will require. None of this is marking time. It is specific preparation.

The step-up introduced in Week 4 Session C is particularly relevant — it is the first single-leg loading pattern in the programme and begins developing the hip stability and single-leg strength that running demands with every stride.

**Running-specific additions to the current block:** None yet in terms of running itself, but two additions to the strength programme are worth making now in light of the running goal.

*Single-leg calf raises:* Introduce these in Week 3 or 4. Standing on one foot, rise onto the toes through full range, lower slowly over 3 seconds. 3 sets of 10 each side. This directly addresses one of the benchmark requirements and builds the posterior chain capacity that running demands. If single-leg is too challenging initially, begin with bilateral and progress.

*Hip abductor work:* The side-lying clamshell is already available as a pallof press substitute. Progress this to a **side-lying hip abduction** — lying on one side, top leg straight, lift to approximately 30 degrees, lower slowly. 3 sets of 12 each side. Strong hip abductors are the primary defence against the Trendelenburg gait pattern — the hip drop on the swing leg side — that is both a running injury risk and a pelvic floor load amplifier.

---

### Block 2 — Weeks 5 to 8 (14–18 Weeks Postpartum)

This is the block that follows the current on-ramp. The running return begins here, but it begins with walking and jogging intervals rather than continuous running.

**Week 5 — 14 weeks postpartum:**

Conduct the full benchmark assessment at the start of this week. Walking, single-leg balance, single-leg calf raise, single-leg bridge — all four non-impact benchmarks. If she passes all four without symptoms, proceed. If not, address the failed benchmarks as training targets and delay the impact introduction by one week.

Assuming she passes: introduce **jog on the spot** as a benchmark test, not a training session. One minute, light pace, on a forgiving surface. Monitor for symptoms during and for 30 minutes after. If symptom-free, she is cleared to begin the walk-run protocol.

**The walk-run protocol — Week 5:**

Three sessions this week, each on a non-strength day or at least 6 hours separated from a strength session. Flat surface, supportive footwear, no hills yet.

Session structure: 5 minutes brisk walk warm-up. Then alternating 1 minute of easy jogging with 2 minutes of brisk walking. Repeat 6 times. 5 minutes easy walk cool-down. Total approximately 30 minutes, of which only 6 minutes is actual jogging.

The jogging pace should feel almost embarrassingly easy — a pace at which she could hold a full conversation without any effort. This is not a fitness session. It is a tissue loading session. The cardiovascular stimulus is irrelevant at this point. What matters is how the pelvic floor, the connective tissue, and the joints respond to the impact load.

**After every run session this week:** Ask her to monitor for symptoms for the following 24 hours. Any leaking, heaviness, pelvic pain, or significant joint soreness that does not resolve within 24 hours means the protocol needs to slow down. One symptom-free session does not mean the next session can be more aggressive — the 24-hour window matters because tissue response to novel load is often delayed.

**Week 6 — 15 weeks postpartum:**

If Week 5 was entirely symptom-free across all three sessions: progress to 2 minutes jogging, 2 minutes walking, repeated 5 times. Same warm-up and cool-down. Total jogging time: 10 minutes.

If Week 5 produced any symptoms: repeat the Week 5 protocol for one more week before progressing. This is not a setback — it is the protocol working as intended.

**Week 7 — 16 weeks postpartum:**

Progress to 3 minutes jogging, 2 minutes walking, repeated 4 times. Total jogging time: 12 minutes. Introduce a very gentle incline — 1 to 2% gradient if on a treadmill, or a gentle slope outdoors — in one of the three sessions. Monitor pelvic floor response to the incline specifically.

Also this week: conduct the impact benchmark tests. Jog on the spot for 1 minute, forward bounds 10 each side, running on the spot for 1 minute, hops 10 each side. These should all be symptom-free before the jogging intervals extend beyond 5 minutes in a single bout.

**Week 8 — 17 weeks postpartum:**

Progress to 5 minutes jogging, 2 minutes walking, repeated 3 times. Total jogging time: 15 minutes. This is a meaningful milestone — she is now running for 5-minute continuous bouts, which begins to feel like running rather than jogging intervals.

Strength programme during Block 2: Continue three sessions per week. The running sessions replace the dedicated cardio sessions — do not add running on top of the full strength programme without reducing something else. A sensible structure is three strength sessions and three run sessions per week, with one full rest day. Total training days: six, with one rest day. This is appropriate volume at 14 to 18 weeks postpartum for a woman who is recovering well.

---

### Block 3 — Weeks 9 to 16 (18–26 Weeks Postpartum)

This is where the running begins to look like actual 10k training. The walk-run intervals give way to continuous running, distance builds progressively, and the strength programme shifts to support running performance rather than simply postpartum recovery.

**The 10% rule applies from this point:** total weekly running volume — measured in either time or distance — should not increase by more than 10% per week. This is standard running injury prevention guidance and applies with particular force in a postpartum return context.

**Week 9 — 18 weeks postpartum:**

Attempt first continuous 20-minute run at an easy conversational pace. If this feels manageable and symptom-free, she has crossed a significant threshold. If 20 minutes continuous is too much, return to 8 minutes jogging, 1 minute walking, repeated twice — the walk break is a tool, not a failure.

**Weeks 10 to 12 — 19 to 21 weeks postpartum:**

Build continuous run duration by 2 to 3 minutes per week. By the end of Week 12 of this block — approximately 21 weeks postpartum — she should be running continuously for 25 to 30 minutes at an easy pace.

**Weeks 13 to 16 — 22 to 26 weeks postpartum:**

Introduce a second weekly run session that is slightly longer than the first. The structure becomes: one easy run of 25 to 30 minutes, one slightly longer run of 35 to 40 minutes, and one optional third session which can be a run or a bike session depending on how the body is responding. By the end of this block she should be running continuously for 40 minutes on her longer run day.

**Strength programme during Block 3:** Shift from three full-body sessions to two sessions per week as running volume increases. The sessions should prioritise the movements most relevant to running performance and injury prevention: single-leg Romanian deadlifts, split squats, single-leg calf raises, hip abduction, and core anti-rotation work. The upper body volume reduces. This is a deliberate trade-off — running is now the primary training stimulus and the strength work is in a supporting role.

---

### Block 4 — Weeks 17 to 24 (26–34 Weeks Postpartum)

Structured 10k preparation. By this point she is approximately 6 to 8 months postpartum, the hormonal environment is considerably more stable, the pelvic floor has had sustained progressive loading, and the training can begin to resemble a conventional 10k programme.

**The key sessions each week:**

*Easy run:* 30 to 40 minutes at a genuinely easy pace — she should be able to speak in full sentences. This builds aerobic base and supports recovery.

*Long run:* The cornerstone of 10k preparation. Build from 45 minutes to 60 to 70 minutes over this block. The long run should also be at an easy pace — the purpose is time on feet and aerobic development, not speed.

*One quality session per week from Week 20 postpartum onwards:* This is where the training begins to have a HIIT-adjacent quality that she has been wanting. Options include:

Tempo intervals — 3 to 4 repetitions of 5 minutes at a comfortably hard pace, roughly 7 to 8 out of 10, with 2 minutes easy between each. This builds lactate threshold, which is the primary physiological determinant of 10k performance.

Hill repeats — find a moderate hill, run up at a hard effort for 60 to 90 seconds, walk or jog back down, repeat 6 to 8 times. Hill repeats build leg strength and running economy simultaneously and are lower impact than flat speed work because the reduced stride length decreases ground reaction forces.

Fartlek — unstructured speed play within an easy run. Pick a landmark and run hard to it, recover, pick another. This is psychologically closer to the interval training she enjoys and is a good introduction to quality work before more structured sessions.

**Do not introduce track intervals or maximal speed work** during this block. The connective tissue adaptation to high-speed running lags behind cardiovascular fitness by several weeks, and the injury risk of fast running on a postpartum body that has not yet built the specific tissue tolerance is meaningful.

---

### Final 6 to 8 Weeks Before Race Day

Standard 10k taper and race preparation. By this point the postpartum-specific considerations have largely given way to conventional running training principles. The main sessions are the long run, one tempo session, and one easy run per week. Volume peaks approximately 3 weeks before race day and then tapers by roughly 20 to 30% in the final two weeks.

A realistic 10k finish time for a woman returning from postpartum at this stage of preparation — assuming she was a competent runner before pregnancy — is likely to be **5 to 10 minutes slower than her pre-pregnancy personal best.** This is not a permanent regression. It is the expected outcome of a return that prioritised health over speed, and the fitness will continue to develop well beyond race day. Setting a time goal that reflects current fitness rather than pre-pregnancy fitness will make the race experience positive rather than disappointing.

---

## The Strength Programme's Role in Running Preparation

This deserves its own section because it is where your expertise as a trainer adds the most value beyond what a generic return-to-running plan provides.

**Single-leg Romanian deadlift:** The most important exercise in the programme for a returning runner. It trains the hip hinge pattern under single-leg load, develops hamstring and glute strength in the position most relevant to the running stance phase, and challenges the lateral hip stability that prevents Trendelenburg gait. Introduce this in Block 2 and keep it in the programme through to race day. Progress from bodyweight to dumbbell load as strength develops.

**Split squat and Bulgarian split squat:** Develops single-leg quad and glute strength through a range of motion that directly transfers to running. The Bulgarian split squat — rear foot elevated — is a particularly high-value exercise for runners because it also addresses hip flexor length, which is commonly restricted in postpartum women due to the sustained hip flexion of feeding and carrying positions.

**Single-leg calf raise with progressive load:** Running propulsion is generated primarily through the calf-Achilles complex. Weak calf raises are one of the strongest predictors of Achilles tendinopathy in returning runners. Progress from bodyweight to weighted — holding a dumbbell at the side — over the course of the programme.

**Hip abduction and external rotation:** Side-lying hip abduction, clamshells, and lateral band walks all target the gluteus medius, which is the primary stabiliser of the pelvis during single-leg stance. Weakness here is the most common biomechanical contributor to running-related pelvic floor symptoms, IT band syndrome, and patellofemoral pain in postpartum runners.

**Core anti-rotation work:** The pallof press, suitcase carry, and farmer's carry from the existing programme are directly relevant to running — the trunk must resist rotation with every stride. Keep these in the programme throughout. As running volume increases, the core work can reduce in volume but should not disappear.

## The Footwear and Kit Conversation

Worth having before she starts running, not after.

**Running shoes:** If her current running shoes are more than 18 months old or have more than 500 miles on them, they need replacing before the return-to-running protocol begins. Postpartum biomechanics are different from pre-pregnancy biomechanics — foot width often increases permanently, arch height can change, and gait patterns may have shifted. A gait analysis at a specialist running shop is worth the time and money, particularly given the 10k goal.

**Sports bra:** Breast tissue changes significantly during and after pregnancy, particularly if breastfeeding. Her pre-pregnancy sports bras are almost certainly not providing appropriate support for running. A high-impact sports bra with good encapsulation — individual cups rather than a compression-only design — is important for both comfort and for reducing the compensatory trunk stiffening that women unconsciously adopt when breast support is inadequate, which has downstream effects on running economy and pelvic floor load.

**Pelvic floor support:** If she experiences any stress urinary incontinence during the early running sessions, a pelvic floor support garment — such as SRC Recovery shorts or similar compression garments designed for postpartum exercise — can provide symptomatic relief while the pelvic floor continues to strengthen. This is a management tool, not a solution — if leaking persists beyond the first two to three weeks of running, it is a referral trigger for the physiotherapist.

---

## If the Race Is in September — The Honest Conversation

If the 10k is in September rather than October or November, the timeline is compressed by four to six weeks and the picture changes meaningfully.

A September race from a current position of 11 weeks postpartum gives approximately 20 to 24 weeks of total preparation. The return-to-running protocol cannot be shortened — the tissue readiness benchmarks are biological, not negotiable. What gets compressed is the structured 10k preparation block, which shrinks from 8 weeks to 4 to 6 weeks. That is not enough time to build the aerobic base and running-specific fitness needed to race a 10k well and safely.

The options in that scenario are:

**Defer the goal to a spring race.** A March or April 10k gives a genuinely comfortable timeline — 28 to 32 weeks of preparation from now, with no compression of any phase. She will race better, feel better doing it, and be at lower risk of injury and pelvic floor setback. This is the recommendation if the September race is not a fixed commitment.

**Enter the September race as a participation goal rather than a performance goal.** Run-walk the entire race, finish it, enjoy it, and treat it as a milestone in the return rather than a competitive event. This is achievable and meaningful without requiring the compressed preparation to produce race fitness. The risk is that the competitive instinct takes over on race day — which it often does — and she runs harder than planned. Have that conversation explicitly beforehand.

**Target a different September event.** A 5k in September is a realistic performance goal from this timeline. The preparation demands are lower, the race itself is shorter and therefore lower cumulative pelvic floor load, and finishing a 5k well at 5 to 6 months postpartum is a genuinely impressive achievement that sets up the 10k goal for spring from a position of strength.

## How to Use This Document

This is the consolidated reference for everything built across the full planning conversation. It does not replace the detailed session notes — those remain the coaching resource. This is the at-a-glance document you can use in session, share with a colleague covering for you, or use as the basis for a client-facing summary. Each week covers the training structure, the intensity parameters, the cardio component, the core focus, and the screening checkpoints.

## Non-Negotiables Across All Four Weeks

These apply regardless of how well any given week goes and do not change in response to positive progress.

Three strength sessions per week maximum. At least one full rest day between sessions. Every session begins with a breath and pelvic floor reset — this is not optional and is not a warm-up formality. No jumping or impact of any kind until after Week 4, per OB instruction. No caloric deficit. No HIIT. Pelvic floor symptoms — leaking, heaviness, dragging, pelvic pain — are an immediate regression trigger at any point. If sleep has been severely disrupted, a session becomes a walk.

## Week 1 — Acclimatisation
### 10–11 Weeks Postpartum

**The Goal**
Reconnect with breath, pelvic floor, and basic movement patterns. Establish a baseline. This is assessment and reintroduction, not a training stimulus in the conventional sense. Nothing is loaded. Nothing is pushed.

**Session Structure**
Three identical sessions across the week. Each session runs 20 to 25 minutes. Sessions are identical by design — repetition builds the neuromuscular habit and gives three comparable data points before anything changes.

Each session contains a 5-minute breath and pelvic floor reset in semi-recumbent, a 5-minute gentle mobility sequence covering cat-cow, child's pose, supine knee-to-chest, and thoracic rotation in side-lying, and a 10 to 12-minute movement reintroduction block.

**Movement Content**
Heel slides, 2 sets of 8 each side. Glute bridge with 2-second hold, 2 sets of 10. Quadruped shoulder taps, 2 sets of 8 each side. Wall push-up, 2 sets of 8. Bird dog Level 1 and 2 introduced at the end of the final movement block — arm only and leg only variations, 2 sets of 6 each side with a 3-second hold.

**Core Focus**
Breath coordination is the core work this week. The heel slides and glute bridges are the load. No additional core block.

**Cardio**
15 to 20-minute conversational walk on non-session days. Pram walking counts. Flat terrain preferred.

**Intensity Parameters**
Perceived exertion ceiling: 4 out of 10. She should feel like she has moved, not like she has trained.

**What to Screen For This Week**

Observe every session for the following and note findings in writing after each one.

Can she find a 360-degree breath expansion — into the sides and back, not just the chest? Can she coordinate a gentle pelvic floor lift on the exhale and a full release on the inhale? Is there any visible doming or coning at the midline during heel slides or quadruped work? Does the lower back stay in contact with the floor during heel slides, or does it arch away as the leg extends? Are the hips level during quadruped shoulder taps, or does the pelvis rotate? Does she report any leaking, heaviness, dragging, or pelvic discomfort during or after sessions?

**Conduct the initial diastasis screen this week, before the first session.**

Resting palpation at three points along the midline — 2 cm above the navel, at the navel, 2 cm below. Note gap width in finger-widths, depth of tissue, and quality of resistance at the base. Active loading test — partial curl-up — watching for doming and feeling for linea alba stiffening response. Note whether breath and pelvic floor cueing improves the midline response. Functional screen — quadruped hold for 5 breath cycles and 5 heel slides each side with observation.

Record findings. If gap is greater than 3 finger-widths with poor tissue tension and doming present, refer to women's health physiotherapist before progressing and keep all work at Week 1 level until seen.

**End-of-Week 1 Question**
Is she moving through the session without symptoms, with reasonable breath coordination, and reporting no adverse effects in the 24 hours after sessions? If yes, proceed to Week 2 as written. If no, repeat Week 1 for one additional week.

---

## Week 2 — Foundation Loading
### 11–12 Weeks Postpartum

**The Goal**
Introduce bodyweight and lightly loaded movement patterns across two distinct sessions. Begin building the session architecture that carries through the block. Pelvic floor coordination remains the primary cue on every exertion.

**Session Structure**
Three sessions per week, 25 to 30 minutes each. Two session types — Session A and Session B — alternating across the week.

**Session A Movement Content**
Glute bridge with 3-second hold, 3 sets of 10. Bodyweight squat to chair, 3 sets of 10. Wall push-up with 3-second eccentric, 3 sets of 8. Dead bug Level 2 or 3 depending on Week 1 findings, 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 8 each side.

**Session B Movement Content**
Romanian deadlift bodyweight or 2 to 4 kg, 3 sets of 10. Reverse lunge bodyweight, 3 sets of 8 each side. Dumbbell bent-over row 2 to 4 kg, 3 sets of 10 each side. Seated dumbbell shoulder press 2 to 4 kg, 3 sets of 8.

**Core Block — Added After Main Sets, Before Cool-Down**
Session A: Dead bug Level 2 or 3, 3 sets of 6 to 8 each side. Bird dog Level 3, 3 sets of 6 each side with 2-second hold. Forearm plank from knees, 3 sets building from 3 to 5 breath cycles.

Session B: Dead bug Level 3 if Level 2 was clean in Session A. Side plank from knees, 3 sets of 15 to 20 seconds each side. Pallof hold — dumbbell at chest or band — 3 sets of 5 breath cycles each side.

**Cardio**
Interval walk introduced — one session per week on a non-strength day. 5 minutes easy, then 6 rounds of 2 minutes brisk walking alternating with 2 minutes easy, 5 minutes easy cool-down. Total 25 to 30 minutes. Flat terrain. Perceived exertion up to 6 out of 10 on the brisk intervals.

**Intensity Parameters**
Strength sessions: perceived exertion 5 to 6 out of 10. Loads are light — the stimulus is pattern quality and time under tension, not load. Rest periods: 60 seconds between lower body sets, 45 seconds between upper body sets. Do not reduce rest periods.

**Mid-Week 2 Intensity Note**
If she is feeling great by mid-week and sessions feel genuinely easy with no symptoms, the following modest progressions are appropriate: slow the eccentric tempo on squats, Romanian deadlifts, lunges, and push-ups to 3 seconds down, 1 second pause, drive up. Increase lower body load to 4 to 6 kg if technique is clean. Introduce single-leg glute bridge if bilateral bridge with 3-second hold is symptom-free. Advance dead bug from Level 2 to Level 3 if midline is behaving well. Move pallof from hold to press. Do not reduce rest periods, do not add sets, do not add a fourth session.

**What to Screen For This Week**

Continue observing every session for doming, breath holding, and pelvic floor symptoms. Specifically this week: does the lower back stay flat during dead bug leg extensions? Are the hips level during single-leg glute bridge if introduced? Is there any midline doming during the plank hold? Does she report any symptoms in the 24 hours after sessions?

Ask at the start of every session: how did you feel after the last session? Any leaking, heaviness, or discomfort? These questions are routine monitoring, not alarm signals, and should be framed as such.

**End-of-Week 2 Checkpoint**
Can she perform a bodyweight squat to the chair with continuous breathing and no midline doming? Can she hold a forearm plank from knees for 5 breath cycles without breath holding? Is the dead bug Level 3 producing a flat lower back throughout? Are all sessions symptom-free during and after? If yes across all four, proceed to Week 3 as written.

---

## Week 3 — Progressive Overload Begins
### 12–13 Weeks Postpartum

**The Goal**
Increase volume modestly, introduce unilateral lower body loading with light dumbbells, progress core to more demanding variations, and introduce the first dedicated cardio session. She should feel like she is working. She should not feel like she is straining.

**Session Structure**
Three sessions per week, 30 to 35 minutes each. Sessions A and B continue. A third session this week can be either A or B depending on scheduling.

**Session A Movement Content**
Single-leg glute bridge, 3 sets of 8 each side. Goblet squat 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 10. Incline push-up hands on table or wall push-up with feet further back, 3 sets of 10. Dead bug Level 3 with 3-second eccentric, 3 sets of 8 each side. Pallof press Level 2 or clamshell substitute, 2 to 3 sets of 8 each side.

**Session B Movement Content**
Romanian deadlift 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 12. Reverse lunge with 2 to 4 kg dumbbells, 3 sets of 10 each side. Dumbbell bent-over row 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 12 each side. Dumbbell lateral raise 2 kg, 3 sets of 10. Seated dumbbell bicep curl, 3 sets of 10.

**Core Block**
Session A: Dead bug Level 3 slow tempo, 3 sets of 8 each side. Forearm plank from toes if Week 2 breathing was clean, 3 sets of 20 to 25 seconds. Suitcase carry 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 15 metres each side.

Session B: Bird dog Level 4 with slow return, 3 sets of 6 each side. Side plank from feet if Week 2 was clean, 3 sets of 20 to 25 seconds each side. Pallof press Level 2, 3 sets of 8 each side.

**Cardio**
One dedicated cardio session per week on a non-strength day. Stationary bike or swimming preferred. 20 to 25 minutes, steady state, perceived exertion 5 to 6 out of 10. Seated cycling only — no standing, no sprints, no high resistance. Alternatively, progress the interval walk to 3 minutes brisk, 1 minute easy, repeated 6 times.

**Intensity Parameters**
Strength sessions: perceived exertion 6 out of 10. Load increases on lower body exercises where technique is clean. Tempo remains slow on main lifts. One session this week can use a circuit format — two or three exercises paired back to back with 75 seconds rest between rounds — to increase cardiovascular demand within the strength session. Apply to one session only this week.

**What to Screen For This Week**

Conduct the second diastasis screen at the start of Week 3. Repeat resting palpation and active loading test. Compare findings to Week 1 baseline. Is the gap the same, narrower, or wider? Is the tissue stiffening response improving? Is doming absent or reduced? Note any changes and adjust programming accordingly.

Benchmark assessment — non-impact: 30-minute brisk walk symptom-free, single-leg balance 10 seconds each side, single-leg calf raise 10 reps each side, single-leg bridge 10 reps each side. All should be symptom-free. Any failures become training targets.

Observe the suitcase carry specifically — any lateral trunk lean toward the weighted side indicates the anti-lateral flexion demand is significant and the load should be reduced.

Monitor the first cardio session carefully. Any pelvic floor symptoms during or in the 30 minutes after the bike or swim session are a regression trigger — return to walking only and reassess.

**End-of-Week 3 Checkpoint**
Can she perform a goblet squat with 4 to 6 kg through full range with continuous breathing and no symptoms? Can she hold a forearm plank from toes for 20 seconds with continuous breathing? Is the suitcase carry producing no lateral lean? Is the dedicated cardio session symptom-free? If yes, proceed to Week 4.

## Week 4 — Consolidation and Bridge
### 13–14 Weeks Postpartum

**The Goal**
Consolidate all patterns from Weeks 1 to 3. Increase session density slightly through an additional set on key exercises. Introduce the step-up as the first dynamic single-leg movement. Prepare the body for a full programme block beginning at Week 5. By the end of this week she reaches 14 weeks postpartum and the OB jumping restriction lifts — though jumping does not enter the programme until Week 5 at the earliest and only after pelvic floor benchmarks are passed.

**Session Structure**
Three sessions per week, 35 to 40 minutes each. Three distinct sessions this week — A, B, and C.

**Session A Movement Content**
Goblet squat 4 to 6 kg, 4 sets of 10. Single-leg glute bridge, 3 sets of 10 each side. Incline push-up, 3 sets of 10. Dead bug Level 3 or 4, 3 sets of 10 each side. Pallof press or clamshell, 3 sets of 10 each side.

**Session B Movement Content**
Romanian deadlift 4 to 6 kg, 4 sets of 10. Reverse lunge with dumbbells 2 to 4 kg, 3 sets of 10 each side. Dumbbell bent-over row 4 to 6 kg, 4 sets of 10 each side. Seated dumbbell shoulder press 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 10. Seated dumbbell bicep curl, 3 sets of 12.

**Session C Movement Content**
Step-up onto sturdy step or bottom stair approximately 15 to 20 cm, bodyweight, 3 sets of 8 each side. Goblet squat 4 to 6 kg, 3 sets of 10. Single-leg glute bridge, 3 sets of 10 each side. Dumbbell lateral raise 2 kg, 3 sets of 12. Dead bug, 3 sets of 8 each side.

**Core Block**
Session A: Dead bug Level 4 with 2 kg dumbbell if Level 3 has been consistently clean. Plank from toes with shoulder tap, 3 sets of 8 taps each side. Suitcase carry 6 to 8 kg if available, 3 sets of 20 metres each side.

Session B: Bird dog Level 4 with 3-second hold, 3 sets of 8 each side. Side plank with top arm reach, 3 sets of 6 reaches each side — or hip dip variation if the reach is too demanding. Pallof press in half-kneeling, 3 sets of 8 each side.

Session C: Plank with leg lift, 3 sets of 6 each side. Side plank from feet, 3 sets of 30 seconds each side. Farmer's carry 6 to 8 kg each hand, 3 sets of 20 metres.

**Cardio**
One dedicated cardio session per week. Stationary bike with mild intervals — 5 minutes easy, 4 rounds of 4 minutes at 6 to 7 out of 10 with 2 minutes easy between, 5 minutes easy cool-down. Total 37 minutes. Alternatively, power walk intervals with gentle incline if available. Perceived exertion ceiling 7 out of 10 on work intervals.
